do_more: Focus on physical, instinctual facial reactions and involuntary bodily shifts (e.g., 'Face Freezes', 'Face Reacts', 'Kids Expect Shock').
Use direct, second-person personal hooks that force immediate self-identification ('Your Face...', 'Your Kids...', 'Your Brain...').
Keep short-form video length tight (around 30 seconds) to maintain high average percentage viewed and trigger re-watches.
Frame public domain book concepts as real-time physiological or emotional phenomena rather than historical citations.
avoid: Avoid dry, academic book titles or reading citations as hooks (e.g., 'The Analysis of Mind', 'Did Munsterberg predict this?').
Avoid abstract, open-ended existential questions that feel like homework (e.g., 'Can the mind be measured?', 'Does class shape your consciousness?').
Avoid vague or broad productivity/money tropes that lack an visceral physiological angle.
short.title_style: High-performing titles use visceral, second-person action statements ('Your [Body Part/Emotion] [Action]') that trigger immediate curiosity about immediate physical reactions.
next_tests: Test a 30-second 'Tight' format script comparing a raw instinctual reaction vs. a historical book citation to directly measure retention drop-off.
Test framing micro-expressions using the winning 'Your [Body Part] [Action]' title formula applied to public domain Darwin concepts.

do_more: Anchor titles to universally relatable bodily sensations or visceral subconscious phenomena (falling dreams, daily habits, facial expressions) rather than abstract cognitive theory.
Prominently feature universally recognizable public-domain authors (e.g., '| Sigmund Freud', '| William James') in the title to provide instant authority and search pull.
Deliver immediate, sensory-driven opening hooks that describe a vivid internal experience instead of generic rhetorical questions.
avoid: Abstract textbook titles, academic section headers, and numbered chapter formats (e.g., 'How We Think · Reading 1').
Lukewarm intellectual queries about social dynamics or attention mechanisms (e.g., 'Why does attention choose focus?', 'Why does your mind amplify group opinions?').
Weak opening lines that start with passive conversational filler like 'You notice your opinions shift... but why does that happen?'
full.title_style: Frame high-curiosity questions around universally experienced physical or subconscious phenomena paired directly with a heavyweight thinker (e.g., 'Why do you dream about falling? | Sigmund Freud').
next_tests: Test visceral subconscious concepts anchored to Freud or Jung (e.g., 'Why do you sabotage your own success? | Sigmund Freud').
Test a dramatic psychological paradox anchored to William James with an abrupt first-sentence hook that skips introductory framing entirely.
full.best_title: Why do you dream about falling? | Sigmund Freud
